newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK party brings anxiety, not cheer, to investors.
newsitem.headline: HK party brings anxiety, not cheer, to investors.

text.p: Hong Kong's historic handover to China will be marked by a five-day period of holiday and festivities but the celebration period has brought anxiety, not cheer, to some investors here, analysts said on Tuesday.

"The market will close for an extended holiday of a five-day duration so people are wondering whether they should hold their positions," said Andrew Fernow, head of research at Vickers Ballas. "If you are a more conservative, risk-adverse investor, you would want to take profit now," he said.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index closed on a loss of 130.27 points, or 0.87 percent, at 14,890.96 on Tuesday, rocked by Monday's 192.25 point decline in the Dow industrials.
The Hang Seng Index had also lost 133.13 points, or 0.88 percent, on Monday following its rise to an all-time high of 15,322.33 points last Friday.
"Since there are five days holiday at the weekend, people are trimming down their portfolios," said Louis Tse, executive director at Standard Capital Brokerage.

Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight of June 30 and the government has declared a public holiday from Saturday to Wednesday to celebrate the event. After Friday's market close, investors will be unable to trade here until next Thursday.

While investor confidence in the market's post-handover prospects remains high, and the handover ceremony on Monday night should see a smooth transition to Chinese rule, analysts said a U.S. Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting next Tuesday and Wednesday could cause some nervousness.

"We are suggesting people be positioned in more defensive stocks over that period and be out of interest-rate-sensitive stocks in case the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) acts or there is some event that crops up in the housing market," said Peter Churchouse, managing director at Morgan Stanley Asia Ltd.
Hong Kong's new government is widely expected to introduce measures soon after the change in sovereignty to cool down rising property prices in the territory.

With investors now nervously watching Wall Street after Monday's drop -- the biggest point fall in the Dow industrials since the Black Monday market crash of October 19, 1987 -- some prefer to reduce their positions altogether and enjoy the holiday, brokers said.
"Investors are worried that if Wall Street has a sharp fall the market will open down (after the handover holiday)," said Howard Gorges, vice chairman at South China Holdings.
But with chances of a U.S. interest rate increase limited, analysts said selling was not heavy in the Hong Kong market and prices could stabilise before the end of the week.
"For the rest of this week it may not necessarily go up," said Percy Au-Young, director of research at DBS Securities.
"But after the handover, a lot of people expect Chinese money to push up the Hang Seng Index. Some people in the market are talking about building up positions ahead of the holiday."
